ITEC board briefing

The building is
part of the course

At Sinclair’s Integrated Technology Education Center, students would see how a change in one classroom affects another. It’s practice for the workplace, where people in robotics, IT, data, and operations have to keep the same systems running together.

Explore workforce skills ↓ Speaker notes

Sinclair's Integrated Technology Strategy brings people from different disciplines into conversation and learning around a shared problem, so students connect technical knowledge with the setting in which it is used. ITEC will provide a dedicated experiential learning facility designed to create these experiences.

The teaching approach

Communication in Context

Each course keeps its own learning objectives. As students see how their work affects other classrooms, they practice explaining what a technical change means for the people who depend on it.

Systems exchange signals

A robot, a sensor, and a controller report what happened at each station. The network carries those signals to the systems that need them.

Students add context

They connect a signal to the work in progress and the people who rely on it. A change at a robot can affect when another class receives a batch, just as it can change when a plant fills an order.

Teams explain a decision

Students explain what changed, what they verified, and why it matters to another team. At work, that explanation helps technicians, supervisors, and operators decide what to check next.

Workforce readiness

What students practice for work

A manufacturer adds a quality check to an automated packaging line. The robot now reports the result, each part takes longer, and the supervisor needs to know when the next batch will be ready. ITEC lets students practice how those teams work through the change together.

Industrial networking & IT
Networking and robotics students verify that a new inspection message travels from the controller to the server. On the job, network technicians work with automation technicians to tell a connection problem from an equipment problem.
Robotics & controls
Students test the new inspection step, measure the time per part, and report what changed. Automation technicians use those checks to verify a line change and explain it to operators and maintenance staff.
Server operations & data analytics
Students in the ISC verify that the server saved the event. Analytics students use SQL to compare cycle times. At work, those checks help a supervisor tell a real slowdown from missing data.
Cybersecurity
In the Teaching SNOC, students practice checking who can view logs or change settings and documenting what needs follow-up. At work, security staff protect access to production systems and coordinate with operations when a change could interrupt the line.
Supply chain & operations
Students compare the line’s output and RFID inventory records, then report when the next batch could be ready. Production and logistics teams use that information to plan receiving, update schedules, and flag discrepancies.

How classes can use the same example

A robotics class could create the records during its regular lab. A networking or analytics instructor can use those records in a separate class to show how its work connects to the same equipment. Try the packaging walkthrough.

Building 8

How a change in one room shows up in another

The Smart Factory and the building’s own systems would give students something real to observe. The classroom network would carry their data to the second-level Instructional Server Center (ISC). The Data Analytics Lab would make it visible on large screens.

Illustrative examples

Follow a change

A robotics class adds an inspection step. During a regular practice run, the controller reports when inspection is complete. The class can follow the event the way a plant team would verify a change before relying on the new production data.

  1. 01 · Generate

    Smart Factory Operations Lab

    The controller reports inspection completion and sends the cycle time.

    Inspection complete
  2. 02 · Carry

    Network Engineering / Fiber Optics Lab

    Networking students work with the robotics team to follow the message from the controller to the servers.

    Message received
  3. 03 · Record

    Instructional Server Center

    Server students verify that the teaching database saved the station, time, and cycle length.

    Cycle time · 12 s → 14 s
  4. 04 · Interpret

    Data Analytics Lab

    A large display shows the change in cycle time. Supply chain students use it alongside output counts to estimate when the next batch could be ready.

    When will the batch be ready?

The building starts a scheduled ventilation cycle. Its heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment reports that a fan has started. Students can compare that event with the temperature trend.

  1. 01 · Generate

    Building HVAC systems

    The facility reports fan status and temperature readings from across the building.

    Fan starts at 9:00 a.m.
  2. 02 · Carry

    Network Engineering / Fiber Optics Lab

    The classroom network makes a read-only feed of facility readings available to the instructional servers.

    Status and readings received
  3. 03 · Record

    Instructional Server Center

    Servers store the fan event and temperature readings so students can compare them by time and location.

    Time and zone recorded
  4. 04 · Interpret

    Data Analytics Lab

    A large display puts the fan event beside the temperature trend. Students can explain what they would ask Facilities to check.

    What changed after startup?

Second level

Inside the Instructional Server Center

The ISC is ITEC’s teaching data center. Rack-mounted servers in this room would receive data from the APT line, the classroom labs, and facility systems such as HVAC.

When a robot reports a completed cycle, students in the ISC could verify that the message arrived, check that the record was saved in the teaching database, and make the data available to the Data Analytics Lab. They would also practice monitoring the servers and tracing a missing record.

Cybersecurity

Two operations centers

Live Sinclair operations

Working SNOC

The Working Security Network Operations Center would actively monitor Sinclair’s cybersecurity. The college’s security team could review real alerts, investigate what happened, and coordinate a response with the teams responsible for affected systems.

Classroom simulation

Teaching SNOC

The Teaching Security Network Operations Center would serve as a classroom. Students could practice reviewing simulated alerts, deciding what needs attention, and explaining the next steps to IT or operations in a training scenario.

How classes use the shared labs

During scheduled classes
A lab might serve a single section over a 16-week term. Instructors can use the connected equipment during regular lessons to show how the disciplines fit together.
Across sections and terms
Faculty can use saved event logs or a recorded demonstration to explore the same change with another class whenever it meets.
Lab support
Faculty, IT, and Facilities oversee access, maintenance, and support. Students can document an observation and discuss what they would check during class.

The APT example

One training line, several disciplines

When an automated line pauses at work, robotics, networking, and operations staff compare what they know before deciding what to do. A class could use the APT training system to examine the same problem from each role’s perspective.

Equipment under consideration

APT Connected Smart Manufacturing System

This is the robotics training system Sinclair is considering for ITEC. APT’s CSM stations can run individually for focused instruction or connect into a full line for a shared project.

In APT’s logistics example, robots mark, assemble, and package parts. Radio-frequency identification (RFID) tags track the parts, programmable controllers coordinate the stations, and a SQL database supports analysis.

View APT’s system details ↗

Illustrative teaching scenario

Why did packaging stop?

In another scenario, a tagged part reaches packaging and the line pauses. See what six roles would check and what each would report to the team.

Training event log

  1. 10:14:02
    AssemblyPart 027 is released.
  2. 10:14:03
    PackagingSensor detects the part.
  3. 10:14:08
    ControllerPackaging pauses while waiting for the part ID.

Is the robot ready?

Robotics students read the robot’s status and check whether it received an instruction to move. They can confirm what the robot was ready to do when the line paused.

What they tell the team “The robot is ready and waiting for a command. Let’s check what the controller needs before it can send one.”

What is the controller waiting for?

Industrial controls students trace the sequence in the programmable logic controller (PLC). The sensor detected a part, and the controller is waiting for a valid ID from the tag reader.

What they tell the team “Packaging detected the part. The next step requires an ID, and the controller is still waiting for it.”

Did the station receive the message?

Networking students confirm the station stayed online during the pause. They work with controls students to check whether the tag reader’s message reached the controller. On a plant floor, those checks help determine which team should investigate next.

What they tell the team “The station stayed connected. We still need to verify whether the reader sent a valid ID.”

Can everyone see the evidence safely?

In the proposed ITEC exercise, cybersecurity students verify that the team can read the training logs and that only designated operators can change machine settings. The Teaching SNOC could use a simulated version of the event to practice explaining a finding to another team.

What they tell the team “Everyone investigating the pause can see the logs. Let’s route any change to the designated operator and record it.”

Can the event records tell us what happened?

Data students use SQL to query the training database. They line up the last confirmed record for part 027 with the next station’s timestamp and check for the missing identification event.

What they tell the team “The timestamps suggest part 027 reached packaging at 10:14:03. We still need the ID confirmation to be sure.”

What should the team do next?

Quality and operations students account for the affected part and decide what evidence they need before it can move forward. They explain their reasoning to the instructor or class.

What they tell the team “Keep part 027 on hold. We need a supervised test that shows the ID is recorded before we release it.”

Read the team’s findings

“Packaging paused while waiting for a valid ID. The sequence points to part 027. The robot was ready and the station stayed connected. Our next step is to check whether the tag reader’s message reached the controller and record the result of a supervised test before releasing the part.”

Supply chain & emerging technology

Follow a product beyond the line

The smart factory could make a real training product for another class to receive. Supply chain students would practice the same checks used on a receiving dock, comparing what arrives with the shipment record before updating inventory.

  1. 01 · Smart factory lab

    Make and pack

    Robotics and controls students could assemble and pack tins of marked parts on the APT line and stage the finished tote for pickup.

  2. 02 · RFID checkpoint

    Tag and verify

    RFID students use readers at the line to verify item IDs. They associate those IDs with a batch and check which items are ready for pickup.

  3. 03 · Between classrooms

    Move the tote

    A proposed autonomous mobile robot (AMR) would carry the tote from the line to a receiving classroom and report pickup and delivery.

  4. 04 · Receiving classroom

    Receive and inventory

    Supply chain students compare the physical count and RFID reads with the expected shipment. They post the verified receipt, record the storage location, and investigate any mismatch.

What the ISC records

ISC students would collect production events from the APT line, reads from the RFID checkpoints, delivery status from the mobile robot, and the receiving record. In a teaching database, they’d use SQL to connect those events by batch or item ID, verify that each step was recorded, and share exceptions with the team that can resolve them. A shared dashboard could show which batches are ready, in transit, received, or on hold.

Illustrative receiving exercise

Did the whole batch arrive?

The delivery status tells us the tote arrived. The receiving team still needs to confirm what’s inside.

The tote contains all 12 items, but one ID didn’t register at receiving. Supply chain holds the receipt, RFID students recheck the tag, and ISC students use the earlier reads to trace the missing ID.

Proposed ITEC workflow. The APT line is under purchase consideration. The mobile delivery robot is a separate proposed addition.

Future readiness

How ITEC can adapt as tools change

The building needs to make it practical for faculty to teach with the next tool and for students to work with people whose expertise differs from their own.

Build for reuse
Plan flexible lab layouts, power and network access, and shared teaching data so programs can add or swap equipment and keep using the same spaces.
Connect existing courses
Faculty can use the same live environment from within their current courses. A robotics instructor might point out the effect of a change on a display. A data instructor could use those same records to teach SQL.
Give new tools real data to work with
As new technology arrives, students could test it against systems they already understand. An emerging technology class might try an AI tool that flags unusual HVAC readings, then verify those flags against the underlying records.

During a regular lab, students can trace a change across equipment, the network, and the servers. They can use the results to explain how the change would affect production or a coworker’s decision.

Speaker notes90-second opening

The building is part of the course because it gives students practice working the way people work after graduation. A plant’s robotics technician, network technician, and production supervisor all depend on the same equipment and data to make different decisions.

Imagine a robotics class adding an inspection step to the packaging line. The instructor can show how the controller’s message reaches the Instructional Server Center. A networking or data class can examine the same records during its own lab, and a supply chain class can use the cycle time to estimate when a batch will be ready.

A lab might serve one section for a 16-week term. Within that class, an instructor can use the connected equipment to show what other teams would see. Faculty can also use a saved example in another section or a later term. Each course keeps its learning goals while students learn how their work informs someone else’s decisions on the job.

How an inspection change travels
